opportunities.title: The OS is the new API layer for agents
opportunities.text: The OS is the new API layer for agents Most mobile operating systems treat AI as an external guest. They treat an agent like a user with a very fast thumb. The agent sits on top of the UI, scraping pixels or poking accessibility services, trying to navigate a world designed for human eyes and tactile input. It is a clumsy, expensive way to work. The AOHP (Android Open use Project) research suggests the mismatch is architectural, not just functional. If you treat agents as first-class OS actors rather than external observers, the efficiency gains are measurable. Preliminary experiments show a 21.12% increase in task completion rate and a 51.55% reduction in token cost compared to conventional systems. But the real consequence is not the efficiency. opportunities.title: Why benchmarking needs a unified interface
opportunities.text: Why benchmarking needs a unified interface Most optimization research is a mess of fragmented workflows. A researcher writes a custom Python script to run an algorithm. They tweak a parameter, run it against a problem, and save a CSV. They do this again for a different algorithm, perhaps using a slightly different loop structure or a different way of handling convergence. They then pull the data into a notebook to run a Wilcoxon test. This is not a standardized pipeline. This is a collection of isolated silos. When every researcher builds their own custom environment, reproducibility becomes a nightmare. opportunities.title: Tools are not the output. The code is.
opportunities.text: Tools are not the output. The code is. Most discussions about AI in development focus on the tools themselves. We talk about model parameters, context windows, and latency. We debate whether a specific agent can solve a specific issue. This focus is misplaced. The tool is just the mechanism. The real signal is the artifact left behind in the source code. The ActuallyTaylor/strata AI dataset shifts the focus from the hammer to the house. It contains 1,325 AI-assisted repositories. This is not a collection of benchmarks or a list of model capabilities. It is a collection of actual work. The dataset includes metadata like repo_id, programming language, star counts, URLs, descriptions, and default branches. opportunities.title: Tooling fragmentation is a runtime problem.
opportunities.text: Tooling fragmentation is a runtime problem. Most polyglot programming research focuses on performance optimizations. They want to make sure the different languages talk to each other without a massive latency penalty. That is the wrong problem for the developer. The real problem is that tooling is trapped behind runtime boundaries. When you try to mix languages using an operating system abstraction or a network connection, you are not just crossing a performance gap. You are crossing a visibility gap. The debugger for language A cannot see the objects in language B. The live inspection tools for language A cannot reach into the heap of language B.
